Choose a gate threshold by Learn-then-Test

Source: R/core-signal-gate.R
hr_gate_threshold.Rd

Finds the loosest threshold on a calibrated signal at which acting on the items whose probability p is at or above it keeps a risk below alpha, with confidence 1 - delta, on the calibration half of the record.

Usage

hr_gate_threshold(
  cal,
  action,
  risk = c("error_among_accepted", "miss_rate"),
  alpha,
  delta = 0.05,
  grid = NULL
)

Arguments

cal

An hr_calibration from hr_calibrate_signal().

action

The action the signal would gate, such as "stop", "skip", "accept" or "exclude". Recorded, and matched against the action of an hr_signal_policy().

risk

"error_among_accepted" or "miss_rate".

alpha

The tolerated risk, strictly between 0 and 1. There is no default: it is a decision about the task, made before the data are seen.

delta

The chance the guarantee fails, strictly between 0 and 1.

grid

Thresholds on the probability scale, in any order; they are tested from the highest down. NULL uses 20 quantiles of p on the fit half (cal$grid).

Value

cal with $gate set: a list of action, risk, alpha, delta, n_min, threshold (NA when none passed), n, k, deff (the design effect), n_eff (n / deff), ucb and coverage (the share of the calibration half acted on) at that threshold, status ("passed", "none passed" or "too few items") and path, a data frame of every threshold with its n, k, deff, ucb, whether it was tested and whether it passed. $status and $reasons are updated.

The procedure

Learn-then-Test (Angelopoulos et al. 2021) with fixed-sequence testing: each threshold t is a hypothesis "the risk at t exceeds alpha", rejected when the one-sided Clopper-Pearson upper bound ucb = qbeta(1 - delta, k + 1, n - k) is at most alpha (1 when k = n), taken on the effective sample described under "Clustered items". Thresholds are tested from strict to loose; the sequence stops at the first that fails, and the loosest one that passed is kept. Because the order is fixed before the labels are looked at, no correction for testing many thresholds is needed.

The risk sets n and k:

"error_among_accepted"

n is the number of items acted on at t (those with p >= t) and k the number of those that were wrong. For actions such as stopping, skipping or accepting.

"miss_rate"

n is the number of items on which acting is wrong (for screening, the eligible records) and k the number of those acted on at t. The denominator does not depend on t. For screening exclusions.

Clustered items

The Clopper-Pearson bound treats items as independent. Items from one document are not: their errors go together, and hr_calibrate_signal() puts part of every document in the calibration half. With n and k taken at face value the guarantee then fails for new documents (with 30 documents of 20 items, a true error rate of 0.12 and an intraclass correlation of 0.3, a gate at alpha = 0.10 and delta = 0.05 passed in 8.7 percent of draws, not at most 5 percent). So the bound is taken on an effective sample: ucb = qbeta(1 - delta, k / deff + 1, (n - k) / deff), where deff, the design effect at that threshold, is the cluster (linearisation) variance of k / n over the calibration half's clusters divided by the variance the same formula gives with each item its own cluster, and is never below 1 (Kish 1965). In the draws above the gate then passed in 2.4 percent of them. Items with no cluster, or in clusters of one, give deff = 1 and the exact Clopper-Pearson bound. So do a single cluster and a threshold with no error (or no right item) among its units, where there is no spread to measure; the bound is then only as good as the assumption that the items are independent. With few clusters deff is itself noisy and the guarantee is approximate.

Even with no errors the bound reaches alpha only from n_min = ceiling(log(delta) / log(1 - alpha)) items: 59 at alpha = 0.05 and 299 at alpha = 0.01, with delta = 0.05. For "error_among_accepted" the sequence therefore starts at the strictest threshold that acts on at least n_min items; that count uses only the scores, not the labels, so starting there keeps the guarantee. For "miss_rate" the set needs at least n_min items on which acting is wrong.

The record becomes "gating" only when a threshold passes and none of the reasons hr_calibrate_signal() gave holds: the graded set had at least 100 wrong items, the fitted map increases with the signal and the ECE used at least 5 bins. Otherwise it stays "advisory" and reasons says why.

References

Angelopoulos, A. N., Bates, S., Candes, E. J., Jordan, M. I. and Lei, L. (2021). Learn then test: calibrating predictive algorithms to achieve risk control. arXiv:2110.01052.

Clopper, C. J. and Pearson, E. S. (1934). The use of confidence or fiducial limits illustrated in the case of the binomial. Biometrika 26(4), 404-413.

Kish, L. (1965). Survey Sampling. New York: Wiley.

See also

hr_calibrate_signal(), hr_apply_signal()

Other signals: hr_calibrate_signal(), hr_calibration_valid(), hr_signal(), hr_signal_policy()

Examples

set.seed(2)
n <- 2000
answerable <- stats::runif(n) < 0.8
score <- stats::runif(n)
graded <- data.frame(cluster = rep(1:200, each = 10), score = score,
                     correct = stats::runif(n) < ifelse(answerable, score, score / 4),
                     answerable = answerable)
key <- list(served_model = "m-2026", version = "2026", task = "qa", format = "pdf",
            prompt_hash = "abc", effort = NA, module = "iterative")
cal <- hr_calibrate_signal("gr.iterative.can_answer", graded, key, seed = 3, B = 0)
cal <- hr_gate_threshold(cal, "stop", alpha = 0.1)
cal$gate[c("threshold", "n", "k", "ucb", "status")]
#> $threshold
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $k
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $ucb
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $status
#> [1] "none passed"
#>
